title: Is halal meat permissible to eat?
headline: The schools differ on meat slaughtered without mentioning Allah's name

summary.text: Meat from a properly slaughtered animal is lawful, and the four schools agree that the food of the People of the Book is permitted. The schools differ on one narrow case: an animal properly slaughtered but over which Allah's name was not spoken. The Ḥanafī and Ḥanbalī schools make the name a condition, the Shāfiʿī school treats it as a sunnah, and the Mālikī school holds it a condition in its well-known position, with a report from Ibn Rushd that it is not a condition at all.

paragraphs.text: The Quran makes the good things lawful, permits the food of the People of the Book, and forbids carrion, blood, swine, what is dedicated to other than Allah, and animals killed without the throat being cut. The prohibition verse reads, "And do not eat of that upon which the name of Allāh has not been mentioned, for indeed, it is grave disobedience" (Quran 6:121). Beside it stands the command, "So eat of that [meat] upon which the name of Allāh has been mentioned, if you are believers in His verses" (Quran 6:118), and the permission, "the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you and your food is lawful for them" (Quran 5:5). The forbidden list in 5:3 adds strangling, blows, falls, goring and what a wild animal has eaten, with the exception "except what you [are able to] slaughter [before its death]", and 6:145 repeats the same four core items, ending with "or it be [that slaughtered in] disobedience, dedicated to other than Allāh".

The most load-bearing report is ʿĀ'ishah's, in al-Bukhārī: people who had only recently left polytheism brought meat, and the questioners did not know whether Allah's name had been mentioned over it; the Prophet said, "You mention the name of Allah, and eat" (Sahih al-Bukhari 7398, also 2057). Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj's report states the positive rule: "Whatever makes the blood flow, and the name of Allah has been mentioned over it, eat it, except for what is slaughtered with a tooth or a fingernail" (Sunan an-Nasa'i 4403). The Prophet sacrificed with the name and the takbīr, Jundab ibn Sufyān heard him say, "whoever has not yet slaughtered should slaughter in the name of Allah", and Shaddād ibn Aws carries the command to sharpen the blade and spare the animal suffering. Abū Thaʿlabah asked about eating from the plates of the People of the Book in their land, and the answer treats their vessels and their food as usable. At Khaybar a Jewish woman brought the Prophet a poisoned roasted sheep and he ate from it.

Two reports carry much of the Ḥanbalī case. The words "the slaughter of a Muslim is lawful even if he does not name Allah, provided he did not do it deliberately" are cited in al-Rawḍ al-Murbiʿ and Kashshāf al-Qināʿ as narrated by Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr. The reply "the name of Allah is in the heart of every Muslim" is cited by Ibn Qudāmah as evidence for the second narration from Aḥmad. The report of the Jews saying "we eat what we kill but not what Allah kills" exists in three routes with three verdicts: munkar in Abū Dāwūd, hasan gharīb in al-Tirmidhī, and a sahih isnād in al-Nasā'ī with the disputants named as polytheists.

The Ḥanafī school makes the name a condition for the animal being lawful, said by the slaughterer over that animal and not by a bystander. A deliberate omission is unlawful, and Ibn ʿĀbidīn says this holds for a Muslim or a kitābī, citing the verse and the consensus of those before al-Shāfiʿī; a qāḍī's ruling otherwise is not enforced. A forgotten omission is lawful, because the Muslim's creed stands in place of the utterance.

The Mālikī school's well-known position is that the name is a condition with remembrance, and Mālik's own formula was "bismillāh wa-Allāhu akbar". A deliberate omission is unlawful on that position, while al-Qarāfī's Dhakhīrah reports two views on the deliberate case and a difference even on the negligent one. A forgotten omission is lawful without dispute, and Ibn Rushd in al-Bayān went further and said the name is not a condition at all, reading 6:121 as carrion not intended as slaughter.

The Shāfiʿī school treats the name as a sunnah, not a condition; al-Nawawī in al-Majmūʿ states that leaving it, deliberately or forgetfully, leaves the animal lawful and entails no sin. Al-Shāfiʿī in al-Umm says that one who abandons it scornfully may not be eaten.

The Ḥanbalī school makes the name a condition with remembrance, dropped in forgetfulness; "bismillāh" specifically, not another name, and it must be at the movement of the hand. A deliberate omission is unlawful, and the Ḥanbalī text adds "even out of ignorance".

The Ḥanafīs and Shāfiʿīs both address the kitābī who names the Messiah while slaughtering: the Ḥanafīs allow it if he meant Allah, and disallow it if he explicitly said "the name of Allah who is the third of three"; al-Shāfiʿī is reported as holding it unlawful if he slaughters for the Messiah, but lawful if the mention was a blessing on the Prophet ﷺ. Mālik disliked what Christians slaughter for their churches and festivals, citing "what is dedicated to other than Allah," while distinguishing that from meat they slaughter to eat.

The sharpest conflict is 6:121 against 5:5. Ibn ʿAbbās held that 6:121 was abrogated and an exception carved out of it by 5:5; Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās took "that over which Allah's name was not mentioned" to mean carrion, not a valid slaughter missing a word; al-Shāfiʿī argued from grammar that "and indeed it is grave disobedience" is a circumstantial clause describing the act, and that the fisq of a slaughter is defined in the Book as what is dedicated to other than Allah. The Ḥanafī answer is that the text is explicit and that the consensus before al-Shāfiʿī settles it, which is why they say a judge may not even enforce a contrary ruling.

The second conflict is 6:121 against ʿĀ'ishah's hadith. The reconciliation nearly everyone uses is procedural: the questioners did not witness the slaughter and had no evidence of a defect, so the act of a Muslim is presumed sound and the doubt is answered rather than investigated. Ibn ʿUthaymīn makes the same move for the People of the Book, while insisting that actual knowledge of an omission removes the presumption.

The Mālikī and Ḥanbalī books distinguish dedicating an animal to something other than Allah from merely forgetting a word, which is why some schools can call the first haram by consensus and still argue over the second. Ibn Rushd reduces the whole disagreement to three positions: an absolute obligation, an obligation waived by forgetfulness, and a confirmed sunnah.

The Permanent Committee in Riyadh held that a mechanical blade is no different from a knife, so if the one moving the machine intends slaughter and names Allah alone the animal is eaten, whether he is Muslim, Jew or Christian (fatwa 4665), and that certifying food as halal is permissible if it truly is, with follow-up required (19873). Ibn Bāz allowed imported meat from non-Muslim countries on the default that it is the slaughter of the People of the Book, unless it is known to have been strangled, hammered or electrocuted, and warned that ʿĀ'ishah's hadith concerns Muslims, so it does not license what is known to be unlawful. Ibn ʿUthaymīn held the default in the slaughter of a Muslim or a kitābī to be lawfulness, without interrogation, and applied that to imported chicken, but said plainly: if you know he did not mention Allah's name, do not eat it.

The Assembly of Muslim Jurists of America allowed chicken in the United States and advised restraint on beef and lamb, because a varying proportion of those animals die from stunning before the throat is cut, and held a halal sign sufficient absent known deceit. The European Council for Fatwa and Research, after a field study, concluded that poultry and beef in Europe are not slaughtered lawfully while lamb and young calves often are. Egypt's Dar al-Ifta treats the slaughter of the People of the Book as lawful by default, with the burden on whoever claims a defect, and excludes meat from idolatrous or atheist lands or meat not slaughtered at all; it also invokes the OIC Fiqh Academy's resolution 95 permitting such meat where the method is unknown. IslamQA states the consensus that the slaughter of idolaters and other non-scriptuaries is unlawful, and that of Christians and Jews lawful unless a defect is known, while cautioning that saying "bismillāh" over meat known to be unlawfully slaughtered does not make it lawful.

On mechanised lines, Ḥanafī-oriented bodies hold that the name must be said by the slaughterer over each animal, so a recorded recitation or one blessing for a batch does not suffice, and Darul Iftaa Chicago added in 2025 that such meat is unlawful to eat but still ritually pure. On stunning, the common thread is that if the stun kills before the cut, the animal is carrion; if it survives and is then slaughtered, the meat is lawful.
